# Data notes

Every count on this page is printed by `src/clean.py` (`data/clean/cleaning_log.json`) and filled in by `src/render_docs.py`.

## Source

- **Dataset:** "Incident management process enriched event log", UCI Machine Learning Repository, dataset 498 (Amaral, Fantinato & Peres, 2018), CC BY 4.0. It's an event log exported from a real ServiceNow instance.
- **File:** `data/raw/incident_event_log.csv`. It has 141,712 events (rows), 36 columns and 24,918 distinct incidents. `run_all.py` downloads it if it's missing.
- **What it does not contain:** free-text descriptions, real category or team names (all labels are anonymised, e.g. "Category 46", "Group 70"), or SLA targets and due times. Only a yes/no `made_sla` flag is included.

## How the event log becomes one row per incident

| # | Decision | Why | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Treat `?` as missing. | It's the dataset's missing-value marker. | Affects many optional fields (problem ID, CMDB item, vendor and others). |
| 2 | Parse dates as day/month/year (`%d/%m/%Y %H:%M`). | Values like `29/2/2016` only parse this way. | No dates failed to parse. |
| 3 | The final state is the **last event by `sys_mod_count`**, with ties broken by `sys_updated_at`. | `sys_mod_count` is ServiceNow's per-record update counter. | 5 events share a counter value with another event of the same incident. The later timestamp wins. Every incident's final state is Closed (24,918). |
| 4 | Keep the 5 events with state `-100`. | They're mid-history events and never the final row. | No effect on the output. |
| 5 | **Time to resolve** = `resolved_at - opened_at`, in hours. | That's the standard definition. | — |
| 6 | If `resolved_at` is blank on the final row, use the timestamp of the incident's last `Resolved` state event. | The field is blank on 1,556 final rows, but most of those incidents do have a Resolved event. | 1,543 filled this way. 13 still have no resolve time and are left blank, so they're excluded from time-to-resolve stats but kept in counts. The `resolved_source` column records which rule applied. |
| 7 | **Met SLA** = `made_sla` on the final event. | The flag changes during an incident's life (it flips to false at breach) in 9,114 incidents, so the final value is the outcome. | — |
| 8 | **Reassignment count** and **reopen count** are taken from the final event. | Both counters only go up. The final value equals the per-incident maximum for every incident (reassignment: yes, reopen: yes). | **Reassigned** = count > 0. **Reopened** = count > 0. |
| 9 | **Assignment group** = the group on the final event, i.e. the group that resolved it. I also keep `first_assignment_group` (the first non-blank group) and `groups_touched`. | This is used for routing analysis. | 2,157 incidents have no group on the final event and are labelled "Not recorded". |
| 10 | Missing category becomes "Unknown". | — | 7 incidents. |
| 11 | **Month** = the calendar month the incident was opened. | Tickets are counted when they arrive. | — |
| 12 | **Reporting window: incidents opened 2016-03-01 to 2016-05-31.** | 98% of incidents were opened in March to May 2016. Outside that range there's one day of February (29 Feb) and a thin tail from June 2016 to February 2017 (5 to 94 tickets a month), which would make the monthly trends misleading. | 481 incidents excluded and 24,437 kept. |
| 13 | Long resolution times are kept, not trimmed. | They're real tickets that stayed open a long time, and trimming them would hide the problem. | 99th percentile = 2,711.2 h. 245 tickets are above it. I report the median next to the mean for this reason. |
| 14 | **Repeat ticket** = the same caller raised a ticket in the same category within the previous 7 days. | It shows recurring demand that reopen counts miss. | 4,814 incidents flagged. |
| 15 | "First line" = **Group 70**, the largest resolving group. | It resolves 38.1% of tickets with a median of 0.2 h, which is the profile of a service desk. **This is an assumption**, because the data doesn't name the teams. | It's used in the root cause analysis. |

## Things to keep in mind when reading the numbers

- **Backlog ramp-up.** The extract starts empty on 1 March, so the open backlog climbs through early March. That climb isn't a real surge. Backlog numbers from April onward are the meaningful ones.
- **March looks very different from April and May.** It has a lower SLA % and much longer resolution times. A large batch of tickets was closed on 24 March 2016 (the single biggest close day), which suggests a clean-up or migration event. I report March as it is but don't read it as a trend.
- **P1 and P2 SLA % is close to zero.** This is what the data says, but with only a few hundred tickets and no SLA targets in the file, it may reflect how the SLA clock was set up for those priorities rather than real performance. I flag it rather than explain it away.
- **Priority** follows the impact × urgency matrix exactly in this data. 94% of tickets are P3 Moderate.
- **"Hours"** are elapsed calendar hours (how long the customer waited), not hours of staff effort.

## Output files (`data/clean/`)

| File | Grain | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `fact_incident.csv` | one row per incident | Excel, Power BI, analysis |
| `dim_date.csv` | one row per day | Power BI |
| `dim_category.csv`, `dim_priority.csv`, `dim_assignment_group.csv` | one row per member | Power BI |
| `metrics.json` | every number quoted in the docs | `render_docs.py` |
| `cleaning_log.json` | every count on this page | `render_docs.py` |
